summary: For ages 6–8, teach that plants need water, light and a suitable temperature to grow and stay healthy by running controlled, one-factor-at-a-time comparisons: a plant deprived of a single need placed beside a thriving control. The concept lives in the CONTRAST over time, with predict-before-observe locking in a guess so a surprising result (pale, leggy, wilted) does the teaching. Anchor in a real first-hand growing comparison; a fast-forward simulation earns its place by compressing a week into seconds so children can run many what-ifs. Keep to the three named factors and avoid soil-as-food framing (addressed later at KS2).
misconceptions: 'Plants get their food from the soil' — the dominant and durable error; at this age keep to water/light/warmth and avoid feeding language, but do not reinforce soil-as-food.
'Plants don't really need light, they just need water' — children over-weight watering (visible care) and under-weight light; the dark-cupboard result is the essential counter.
Thinking a plant in the dark that is still green/standing is 'fine' — needs longer observation to see it go pale and leggy (etiolation).
Believing plants need exactly the same conditions as animals (e.g. must be warm/indoors), missing that 'suitable' varies by plant.
Assuming more of a good thing is always better (drowning a plant with water, scorching heat) rather than 'suitable' amounts.

activities.title: Windowsill vs cupboard: a real cress comparison
steps: Start with two identical pots of young green cress (or bean) seedlings, keep both soils similarly moist, and put one on a bright windowsill and one in a dark cupboard.
Before waiting, write or say a prediction: how will each plant look after a week, and WHY?
Keep a growth diary: draw the same plant on day 1, 3, 5 and 7 to make the slow change visible.
After a week, describe the result and name which single need was missing for the cupboard plant.
activities.insight: Light is a genuine growth need, not an optional extra — watering alone does not keep a plant healthy. Over days the dark plant goes pale, leggy and floppy while its watered twin in the light stays green and sturdy.

activities.title: Grow-lab: one dial at a time
steps: Use a fast-forward grow-lab (or an adult-run paper/role-play version) with two identical seedlings: a 'test' plant you can change and a 'control' you keep fixed.
Change ONLY ONE thing on the test plant — turn its light off (or bright/dim), give it no water or lots of water, or make it cold/warm/hot — and leave everything else the same as the control.
Lock in a prediction, then start the grow so days tick past in seconds and watch how the test plant responds.
Run it again with a different single dial (water, then temperature) and compare each result to the healthy control.
activities.insight: When you change one factor and keep the rest the same, you can pin the effect to that factor. Each missing need produces a recognisable result: dark → pale and leggy; no water → wilted and dry; cold → stunted growth.

activities.title: Match the cause to the effect (recap/reference)
steps: Study a before/after set pairing each deprivation with its symptom: dark → pale and leggy; no water → wilted and dry; cold → stunted.
Tap or point to a pale cupboard-plant, a wilted dry plant, and a healthy control and say which need each one had or lacked.
Match condition icons (watering can, sun, thermometer) to the plant outcomes.
Use a 'how much water is suitable?' choice to show that more is not always better — too much drowns, too little dries.
activities.insight: Each of the three named needs has a distinct effect when missing, and 'suitable' means a right amount — not maximum. The healthy control shows what all three together look like.

checkQuestion: I have two identical little cress plants. One I keep on a sunny windowsill and water it; the other I put in a dark cupboard but still water it. After a week, will they look the same or different — and the important part, WHY? What does the cupboard one miss out on?
checkAnswer: Different: the windowsill plant grows healthy and green; the cupboard plant grows pale, spindly and weak (or dies) because it has NO LIGHT. Plants need light (as well as water and a suitable temperature) to grow and stay healthy — water alone is not enough. Full marks name light as the missing need and predict the unhealthy outcome.
